title: “I Never Knew You”: The Terrifying Truth About Lawlessness in Matthew 7:23
paragraphs:
“I Never Knew You”: The Terrifying Truth About Lawlessness in Matthew 7:23
The Greek Word That Should Shake Every Christian Awake
There are few words Jesus ever spoke that strike the human heart with greater force than the chilling declaration found near the end of the Sermon on the Mount:
“Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness.’” (Matthew 7:23)
Stop for a moment.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ after a lifetime of religious activity.
You preached.
You served.
You prayed.
You sang worship songs.
You attended church.
You called Him “Lord.”
And yet the King of Kings looks into your eyes and says:
“I never knew you.”
Not “I knew you once.”
Not “I knew you but you drifted away.”
Not “I knew you and forgot.”
“I never knew you.”
Few passages in Scripture expose the difference between religious appearance and genuine relationship more powerfully than this one.
And everything hinges on a single word.
Lawlessness.
Most people think they understand what Jesus meant.
Most do not.
Because the deeper meaning is far more personal, far more dangerous, and far more relevant than many realize.
The Greek word Jesus used is ἀνομία (anomia).
It comes from two parts:
“a” meaning “without,” and
“nomos” meaning “law.”
Literally, it means “without law.”
But Jesus was not merely describing criminals breaking rules.
The word carried a much deeper meaning.
In biblical Greek, ἀνομία (anomia) describes a condition of rebellion against God's authority—a heart that refuses His rule even while claiming association with Him.
This is why Jesus was not addressing atheists.
He was addressing religious people.
People who publicly acknowledged Him.
People who used His name.
People who appeared spiritual.
The warning is not aimed at those outside religion.
It is aimed at those who look religious while secretly living independent of God's authority.
This becomes even clearer when we examine the Hebrew background behind Jesus' teaching.
Jesus spoke primarily within a Jewish context deeply rooted in the Hebrew Scriptures.
The Hebrew concept closest to this idea is עָוֹן (avon) and sometimes פֶּשַׁע (pesha).
These words describe more than wrongdoing.
They describe twistedness, rebellion, defiance, and deliberate departure from God's ways.
Psalm 51:5 uses עָוֹן (avon) when David cries out over his sin.
Isaiah repeatedly uses פֶּשַׁע (pesha) to describe rebellion against God.
The issue is not simply that someone sinned.
Every believer sins.
The issue is whether someone is surrendered.
Whether someone bows before God's authority.
Whether someone truly belongs to Christ.
This distinction changes everything.
Because Matthew 7:23 is not teaching salvation by perfect performance.
If that were true, nobody would survive Judgment Day.
The Bible repeatedly teaches salvation by grace through faith.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8-9)
The problem in Matthew 7 is not imperfect believers.
The problem is people who wanted the benefits of Jesus without submission to Jesus.
Notice what they say:
“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and cast out demons in Your name, and do many mighty works in Your name?” (Matthew 7:22)
Their defense is fascinating.
They present achievements.
Accomplishments.
Ministry successes.
Religious résumés.
But Jesus points to relationship.
Not performance.
Not influence.
Not public recognition.
Relationship.
The Greek word for “knew” here is ἔγνων (egnōn) from γινώσκω (ginōskō).
This word often describes intimate, personal, relational knowledge.
Jesus is not saying He lacked information about them.
God knows everything.
He is saying they never belonged to Him in a covenant relationship.
They knew religion.
But they did not know Him.
And perhaps that is one of the greatest scandals in church history.
People can know sermons and never know the Savior.
People can know theology and never know Christ.
People can know ministry and never know intimacy with God.
People can know church culture and still be strangers to Jesus.
That reality should humble every one of us.
Because lawlessness is often much more subtle than open rebellion.
Sometimes lawlessness looks respectable.
It appears in the person who worships publicly but refuses forgiveness privately.
It appears in the person who speaks Christian language while nurturing secret sin.
It appears in the person who wants Christ as Savior but not Christ as King.
It appears whenever we say, “Lord,” with our lips while withholding areas of our lives from His authority.
The danger is not merely breaking God's commands.
The deeper danger is resisting God's rule.
This is why Jesus had already warned earlier in the chapter:
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of My Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)
The evidence of genuine faith is not perfection.
It is surrender.
Not sinlessness.
But repentance.
Not flawless obedience.
But a transformed heart that continually returns to Christ.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if Matthew 7 only exposed us, it would leave us hopeless.
The truth is that every one of us has traces of lawlessness within us.
Every one of us has resisted God.
Every one of us has wandered.
Every one of us has fallen short.
The Hebrew Scriptures call this reality חֵטְא (chet)—missing the mark.
The Apostle Paul echoes this truth:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
The story does not end there.
Because Jesus did not come merely to expose lawlessness.
He came to rescue lawless people.
Titus 2:14 says that Christ:
“gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.”
Notice that.
Not simply forgive lawlessness.
Redeem us from it.
Transform us through it.
Deliver us out of it.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely improve bad people.
He resurrects dead people.
He does not merely adjust behavior.
He transforms hearts.
He does not merely offer second chances.
He creates new creations.
And this is exactly why our theme remains so powerful:
Because the greatest scandal is not the sins we've committed.
The greatest scandal is that the holy Son of God willingly took our judgment upon Himself.
At the cross, the perfectly obedient Christ bore the punishment deserved by lawless sinners.
There, justice and mercy embraced.
There, grace triumphed.
There, the story was rewritten.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying secret shame.
Perhaps there are failures nobody knows.
Perhaps there are compromises hidden beneath a polished exterior.
Perhaps you fear what God sees when nobody else is watching.
Hear this carefully:
The Gospel is not an invitation to hide better.
It is an invitation to come home.
Jesus does not save people because they cleaned themselves up.
He saves people who surrender.
People who repent.
People who trust Him.
People who admit they need Him.
That is why Matthew 7 should not merely terrify us.
It should drive us into the arms of Christ.
The answer to lawlessness is not trying harder.
The answer is knowing Jesus and being known by Him.
And that relationship changes everything.
Your testimony may be the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
One day every title, every accomplishment, every platform, every achievement, and every earthly applause will disappear—but the words “Well done” from Jesus will echo forever.
